paper_title: From RL Papers to Framework Code: Inclusion and Review in Seven Open-Source Training Frameworks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Practitioners use reinforcement learning methods for language models through training frameworks, so a method that a framework includes is one configuration change away for its users. We measure how often this happens. We trace seven open-source frameworks for RL post-training through their commit histories and link them to 6,939 screened arXiv papers from January 2025 to June 2026. Of 1,598 papers that propose a general RL training method, 37 reached at least one framework. Across five quarterly cohorts of papers, the number included within 180 days stayed between 5 and 7 while the cohorts grew from 72 to 386 papers. Compared with papers from the same quarters, included papers more often trained policies of 30B parameters or more, at 41 against 10 percent, and more often changed a coefficient, clip, mask or weight in the existing loss, at 29 against 9 percent. Both gaps hold without papers from the companies that maintain the frameworks, while code release was equally common in both groups. The frameworks' issues and pull requests show that few methods are turned away in public. More than nine in ten of the general methods no framework included have no thread there that cites or names them, and many proposals that do appear stay open without a reply. Two further records, the frameworks' issues and the technical reports of 13 large open-weight models, show that users rarely report training failures in public and that the reports state 8 of the 13 widely included methods. We release the data as a tracker that links training failures to framework implementations and lists each framework's contribution rules and earlier proposals.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: GSPO [88] reached TRL 3 days after its first arXiv version, and verl, OpenRLHF, ROLL and slime followed within week. All seven frameworks in this study include it today. In the same month, 43 other papers proposed general RL training method for language models, and only 2 of them reached any of the seven frameworks. Research on RL post-training has grown fast: in each month of the first half of 2026, at least 144 papers in our pool proposed an RL training method. Practitioners meet these methods through the frameworks they train with, and framework decides whether method is one configuration change away or separate project. Publishing method, releasing its code and having framework include it are three separate outcomes, and the last one has not been measured. We measure framework inclusion. method counts as included when its implementation reaches the main branch of tracked framework, and we record the tier of each inclusion: default, selectable algorithm, switch, experimental code or an example recipe. Inclusion describes the code that frameworks ship, and Section 11 sets out its limits. Technical report, version 1, 20 October 2026. Data and code: https://github.com/pth2002/rl-method-tracker, archived as doi:10.5281/zenodo.23495743. Figure 1: Inclusion, supply against intake, and the public record of the rest. Unit: paper. (a) Papers from January 2025 to June 2026: the screened pool, papers that propose an RL training method, general methods, and general methods by the strongest inclusion they reached, on log scale. (b) General methods by the quarter of their first arXiv version in grey, and those framework included within 180 days of that version in blue, for the quarters with 180 days of exposure before the snapshot for every paper, on log scale. (c) General methods that no framework included, grouped by the threads in the seven frameworks that link them, give their identifier or quote their title, on log scale. These groups are categories and not stages. Inclusion is rare: only 37 of 1,598 papers that propose general method reached one of seven frameworks (2.3 percent). The included methods differ from the rest in two ways (Section 6). Their papers more often trained policies of 30B parameters or more, at 41 against 10 percent, and more often changed coefficient, clip, mask or weight in the existing loss, at 29 against 9 percent. Code release was equally common, at 44 percent of included papers and 44 percent of others. The two gaps persist without model reports, within papers that have an industry author, and without papers from the companies that maintain the frameworks. They remain associations, and Section 6 sets out their limits. The intake did not keep pace with the supply. Across five quarterly cohorts, the number of general methods framework included within 180 days stayed between 5 and 7, while the cohorts grew from 72 to 386 papers, 5.4-fold rise (Figure 1b). Counted by the date of the landing instead, first landings of general methods rose from 3 quarter at the start of 2025 to 10 at its end. The frameworks took in more methods as the supply grew, but shrinking share of each cohort. Few of the other methods were turned away in public. We collected the issues, pull requests and discussions of all seven frameworks and searched them for every general method in the pool. Maintainers declined or redirected proposals for only 12 of the 1,561 general methods that no framework included. Most never came up in frameworks issues or pull requests at all: 96 percent have no thread that cites them (Figure 1c), and search by method name lowers this only to 95 percent. Many proposals that do appear stay open without reply. Merged pull requests also drew concerns, mostly about design and tests, and their authors often revised the code in response. Concerns about demand and maintenance burden appear mostly in proposals that were not merged, and most of those come from one framework (Section 7). Two further records place inclusion next to users and to large training runs. In the frameworks issues and discussions, 48 of the 7,075 threads opened since January 2025 report training failure, and the failures they name are distributed differently from those that paper abstracts address (Section 8). Technical reports of 13 open-weight models with 100B parameters or more state 8 of the 13 widely included methods, describe variants of others under their own names, and are the source of 2 (Section 9). We release the data and code as tracker. Its index links training failures, such as entropy collapse or mismatch between rollout and training probabilities, to the implementations and settings in each framework. second page gives each frameworks contribution rules, the concerns its reviewers raised and the outcome of earlier proposals, as starting point for authors who want framework to include their method.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Studies of industry and academia in AI mostly work at the level of papers and topics. They track the growing share of industry in AI research [2] and the association between code availability and citation counts [90]. Forks of the repositories that accompany ML papers rarely change the code, and fewer send changes back [5]. These measures capture attention among researchers but do not observe whether method reaches the code that trains models. second line asks whether reported gains hold up. Re-evaluations in recommendation [12] and metric learning [50] found that many improvements vanished under careful comparison, and broader critiques point to benchmark selection [15] and scholarship practice [38]. Implementation details matter as much in policy-gradient methods: code-level choices explain much of the reported gap between PPO and TRPO [17], and an implementation guide lists 37 such details for PPO alone [29]. For RL with language models, controlled studies compare tricks under one implementation [44] and test methods at large compute [31]. These studies ask whether method works. We ask whether frameworks include it, and we read the answer from their code. third line studies the decisions of open-source projects on outside contributions. Only few factors drive the decision to merge pull request, and few rejections are technical [23]. Project managers weigh technical signals together with their social ties to the submitter [72], and integrators report trouble keeping quality high and ranking the contributions they receive [24]. Reviewers also look at signals beyond the code [19], and ties across an ecosystem shift acceptance [46]. These studies explain decisions about code contributions in general. We follow narrower object: method from paper, traced from its evidence to its implementation in training framework and to the public record of each proposal.

sections.title: 3 Measuring inclusion
sections.content: Frameworks. We study verl [64] with its recipe repository, TRL [74], OpenRLHF [27], NeMo-RL [51], ROLL [76], slime [92] and AReaL [20]. All seven meet four criteria: they are built for RL post-training of language models, run their own training loop with several selectable RL algorithms, are developed in public, and have at least 2,000 GitHub stars. Four other frameworks meet the same criteria: open-instruct, SkyRL, prime-rl and RLinf  (Table 10)  . At their latest commits they implement 2 general methods that none of the seven include, so adding them would raise the inclusion rate from 2.3 to 2.4 percent. The snapshots of six frameworks date from 13 to 17 October 2026. OpenRLHF had no main-branch commit after 17 September 2026, so its snapshot is older  (Table 10)  . Algorithm locations. Each framework exposes its RL algorithms in few places. verl registers advantage estimators and policy losses by name, while TRL selects GRPO losses through loss-type field and keeps newer trainers in an experimental folder. AReaL ships one example configuration per algorithm, and the other frameworks use command-line choices and configuration switches. We list these places for each framework, parse them at every commit on the main branch, and check the result against each frameworks algorithm documentation at the snapshot. Tiers. We record the tier of each inclusion. default is on in run that keeps every setting. conditional default is on by default once related feature is enabled, such as generation with vLLM. core option is selectable algorithm in the main code path, and switch modifies the main algorithm. Experimental code and example recipes sit outside the main path. From options to methods. Frameworks name the same method differently: clip-higher [84] appears as clip_ratio_high in verl, epsilon_high in TRL, eps_clip_low_high in OpenRLHF and eps-clip-high in slime. We map every option name to one entry in catalog of 65 methods and check each source against its arXiv record. The parser reports every option it detects without mapping, and the build fails until the option is mapped. An event is the addition or removal of an option, or change of its default, on main branch, and the history of the seven frameworks yields 426 events. Implementations outside the parsed places are the target of the documentation check and of the citation audit below. 3 Citation audit. Parsing misses an implementation that sits under name the catalog does not map, in place we do not parse, or in change to existing code. We therefore searched the full main-branch history of each framework for the arXiv identifiers of pool papers and kept every file that cites one. Framework files cite 51 general methods, including all 28 that parsing had found. For 9 of the other 23, citation sits next to an implementation, and we added them to the catalog. Two of them add no option: fix to the KL gradient in NeMo-RL and the trajectory-level agent pipeline of ROLL. We record such implementations from their commits, so the implementation stays the test of inclusion. The remaining papers appear in lists of projects built on framework, in reference lists of technical reports, or as background (Appendix E). Dates. date is the commit date on the main branch, an approximation of the day change became available there. An option first seen in repositorys root commit, in bulk code release, or in commit that renamed an existing option has an unknown start, so we treat such date as an upper bound. landing is the first commit that brings method into one framework, and the first landing of method is its earliest landing in any framework. later exact date from another framework never replaces an earlier upper bound. Lags run from the first arXiv version of the source, or from the post date for blog sources. People. For each landing we compare the git author of the introducing commit with the author list of the source. The comparison has four outcomes: paper author, named person outside the list, handle we cannot resolve, and source without an author list. When the commit names pull request, we also record who opened it, who merged it and who reviewed it. We call person prior merger of framework once they have merged pull request there, comparing UTC timestamps with the event in question. Prior mergers stand in for maintainers, but the proxy misses reviewers without merge rights and people before their first merge, and it keeps people who have since left. We also match the affiliations on each papers first page against the company that maintains each framework, such as ByteDance for verl and NVIDIA for NeMo-RL. OpenRLHF has no maintaining company.

sections.title: 4 Measuring the supply of methods
sections.content: Screening. Keyword search through the arXiv API misses papers that typeset method names in LaTeX. The DAPO abstract, for example, writes its name through bold initials. We therefore harvest the complete computer science metadata through the arXiv OAI-PMH interface and keep the 139,135 records in cs.LG, cs.CL or cs.AI with identifiers from 2501 to 2606. paper enters the pool when its title or abstract mentions language models and reinforcement learning, including the abbreviations RL and RFT. The pool holds 6,939 papers and contains 45 of the 46 catalog sources from this window. This check covers included sources only, so the pool is screened set and not complete census of RL papers. Labels. Each paper receives one of seven labels from its title and abstract under fixed rules (Appendix A). The label of interest marks new or modified training-time RL component. We call such method general when the component is the papers main contribution and is presented for RL with language models at large. We call it embedded when it serves paper about one task, domain or application. The denominator is the set of general methods. Checks. Three checks address recognition, stability and the general rule. For recognition, the included sources were mixed into the first batches without marking, and 29 of the 30 sources not used as examples in the labelling rules were labelled as methods. The miss is technical report that describes its method only in the body. For stability, 140 papers were labelled twice in separate batches and kept the same primary label 129 times. For the general rule, stratified sample of 200 papers was reviewed manually. Review and labels agree on 188 of them for the split between general methods and all other papers, and weighting by the three label strata puts the number of general methods at about 1,590 (Appendix B). Model reports. Technical reports for new models often describe their RL changes only in the body, so we read 70 randomly drawn reports in full. The sample holds 30 reports labelled as methods and 40 labelled otherwise, and it leaves out reports with included methods. transferable RL component appears in the body of 25 reports of the first group and 6 of the second. The general rule asks for more 4 Figure 2: Time from first public version to main branch. Unit: catalog method with dated source from 2025 or later that reached two or more frameworks. Figure 5 in the appendix shows every method. Each mark is one landing. Hollow dots mark commits by paper author. Crosses mark landings in bulk release or renaming commit, and their dates are upper bounds. Landings within few days of each other are spread vertically within their row. The larger mark with number counts landings too close to draw apart: five frameworks took in GSPO between 3 and 7 days after its first version. than transferable component, so these counts bound the effect of abstract-only labels from above. Counting every report with such component as general method would raise the denominator by at most about 13 percent and lower the inclusion rate from 2.3 to 2.1 percent.

sections.title: Inclusion rate
sections.content: Few general methods reach framework. Figure 1a follows the pool from all RL papers to framework defaults: 37 of 1,598 general methods reached at least one framework, rate of 2.3 percent. Three or more frameworks include 7 of them today, and 1 is an unconditional default. Many methods were brought in by people outside the author list. For 18 included papers, at least one landing came from named commit author outside the papers author list. Another 12 reached frameworks only through commits by their authors, and the remaining 7 only through unresolved handles or sources without an author list. Another 8 included papers fall outside the general rule from their abstracts. Most are model reports or system papers with an included component in the body (Appendix D). Adding them gives 45 included papers out of 1,606, with 9 in three or more frameworks. Exposure time matters: papers from 2025 had at least nine months before the snapshot, and 31 of 769 reached framework. Papers from the first half of 2026 had less time, and 6 of 829 did. sections.title: 6 Features of included methods
sections.content: Figure 3 compares the 31 included general methods from 2025 with 150 general methods from the same year that no framework included. The controls were drawn at random within each quarter, and fields were coded from the first arXiv version of each paper without access to inclusion status (Appendix C). The citation audit found 8 of the included papers later, and second reader recoded these papers blind. The comparison uses the blind codes, and Table 7 gives the gaps without them. The comparison is descriptive, because scale, resources, team composition and breadth of experiments can vary together. The figure shows every coded field. We single out two of them because they have the largest ratio between the groups among the fields that at least five papers show in each group. Mixture-of-experts policies differ by larger ratio, but they appear in only 3 included papers and 1 other. 6 Figure 3: Coded fields, included against non-included general methods from 2025. Unit: paper. Each row compares the share among included papers with the share among papers from the same quarters that no framework included. The right columns give the counts, included first. Two shares within three points of each other are drawn one above the other. Papers that do not report property are left out of that row. Scale shows the largest gap. Policies of 30B parameters or more appear in 41 percent of included papers and 10 percent of the others. The gap persists after excluding model reports, at 12 of 29 against 13 of 139, and within papers that have an industry author, at 10 of 25 against 11 of 90. Counting every unreported size against the gap still leaves 12 of 31 against 23 of 150. The form of the change also differs. coefficient, clip, mask or weight in the existing loss was the change in 29 percent of included papers and 9 percent of the others, while new training stage or model was the change in 26 against 53 percent. The frameworks expose the widely included methods in the same compact form: one or two configuration fields or loss names, such as clip_ratio_high in verl and epsilon_high in TRL for clip-higher  (Table 11)  . The compact form describes the method and not the size of its code, because pull requests for coefficient changes were about as large as those for new loss terms (Section 7). The number of new hyperparameters is missing for many papers, and under the least favourable treatment of missing values its gap reverses, so we do not interpret it. The two gaps hold outside the frameworks own companies. Included papers come from company that maintains one of the frameworks more often than others, at 32 against 15 percent, but only 5 were included by that companys framework. Across all 37 included papers, 11 come from such company and 6 were included by its own framework, such as DAPO in verl and DLER in NeMo-RL. Inclusion also crosses company lines through the people who commit: all 18 papers with an outside committer had such landing in framework outside their own company. Without any such paper in either group, large policies appear in 6 of 19 included papers against 9 of 119 others, and coefficient changes in 6 of 21 against 13 of 128  (Table 7)  . Code release was equally common in both groups. The first version links training code in 44 percent of included papers and 44 percent of others, so public implementation alone does not set the included methods apart. Other fields point the same way as the main gaps with smaller differences. named training failure motivated 84 percent of included papers and 70 percent of others, and evaluation beyond one domain appears in 55 against 48 percent of them. Industry authors appear on 90 percent of included papers and 64 percent of others, while included papers reported compute less often, at 19 against 29 percent. Inclusion also differs by component (Figure 4). Methods that change clipping or the trust region, off-policy correction, or loss aggregation make up 187 of the general methods, and 10 of these reached framework, 3 of them three or more. Rollout sampling is the most crowded component. Together with credit assignment it accounts for 554 general methods, 4 inclusions and none in three or more frameworks. This comparison covers framework options only (Section 11). 7 Figure 4: Inclusion by component. Unit: general method, each with one primary component label. Share of general methods in each component that reached at least one framework, with counts. Rows are ordered by the number of general methods, and components with fewer than ten are omitted. Most of the widely included methods are motivated by failure that appears in long or large runs: entropy collapse, length bias, extreme importance ratios, instability in mixture-of-experts models, and the mismatch between rollout and training probabilities  (Table 1)  .

sections.title: 8 Failures that users report
sections.content: The frameworks issues are where users would report the failures that the catalogs methods address, so they record what users name in public. We screened the 7,075 issues and discussions opened in the seven frameworks between January 2025 and the snapshot with keyword patterns for the thirteen failures of the catalog, and one reader coded the title and opening post of each of the 648 matches (Appendix E). thread counts when its opener reports observing the failure in run. Most matches were bugs, usage questions or feature requests, and 48 threads report training failure  (Table 4)  . Among them, 23 describe collapse or divergence with no cause named, such as loss that turns to NaN or reward that drops to zero, and 12 name the mismatch between rollout and training probabilities. random sample of 250 unscreened threads, read the same way, contained no failure report. The failures named in public differ from those that papers address. The failures that abstracts address most often, sparse reward in 218 general methods and the loss of diversity in 156, appear in no screened thread. The mismatch between rollout and training probabilities is named by 12 threads, and 20 general methods and 8 catalog methods in the frameworks address it, more than for any other failure. The record measures what users name in public and not what they need, because an abstract and an issue serve different purposes and the 23 collapses with no cause named may belong to any row of the table. sections.title: 11 Limitations
sections.content: Inclusion is not use: we observe implementations on main branches, and the data do not show the frequency of use or the results users get. Section 9 reads what 13 reports state, and statement in report is not code either. The numerator is lower bound, because it counts only options we can parse and implementations that framework files cite. Sampling and reward logic can live outside framework options, so the component comparison covers framework options only. The pool is screened from three arXiv categories, and the seven frameworks represent neither closed training stacks nor every open one. Four other open frameworks meet the selection criteria, and their current code adds 2 general methods to the included set (Section 3). The comparison in Section 6 is observational and small. Affiliations come from each papers first page and match framework at the level of the company, so team that works with frameworks maintainers from another company counts as outside. The public record misses chat groups and internal repositories, and the search by method name reaches only names that are distinctive. ROLL and AReaL publish much of their code in bulk releases. Landings without pull request still went through review, and the pull requests with record do not represent each frameworks whole process. Thread texts can be edited or deleted after the fact, and one reader coded the review fields of all threads. The failure reading of Section 8 covers titles and opening posts after keyword screen, by one reader, so its counts are lower bounds, and collapse reported without cause may belong to any of the failures. The reports of Section 9 cover 13 models from nine organisations and state what their authors chose to write. Whether maintainers act on such reports, on requests or on their own runs is not measured here, so the overlap between the reports and the frameworks code is an observation and not direction of influence.

sections.title: 12 The tracker
sections.content: The data and code behind this report form maintained tracker at https://github.com/pth2002/ rl-method-tracker. Its index groups the catalog by the training failure each method addresses. For every method it shows the frameworks that include it, the tier and the day it landed, with the setting that selects the method and link to the file and line at the analysed commit. second page gives, for each framework, its contribution rules, the files that hold its algorithms, the pull requests that brought recent methods in, the concerns raised in their review and the outcome of earlier proposals. Readers can report wrong record through correction form in the repository. weekly job pulls the frameworks, re-traces their history, verifies sources against arXiv and opens pull request. An option the parser detects without mapping fails validation, so person reviews every addition before it reaches the index. The release fixes the samples, labels, full-text coding and framework commits behind this report, together with checksum list. It also stores the record of proposals. For each general method it lists the issues and pull requests that cite it, their state at the snapshot and the coded outcome. Thread texts stay on GitHub, and each coded thread keeps one short quote as evidence for its code. The release also stores the coded failure reports of Section 8 and the readings of the model reports of Section 9, each with one quote. The weekly job also refreshes this record and lists new proposals for coding. separate command checks the inputs against that list and reproduces the reports numbers, tables and figures without network access.

sections.title: 13 Conclusion
sections.content: Most RL methods for language models reach practitioners as papers and not as options in the frameworks they train with. Between January 2025 and June 2026, 2.3 percent of the general RL training methods in our pool reached one of seven open-source frameworks, and three or more frameworks include 7 of 1,598 today. Across five quarterly cohorts the papers grew 5.4-fold while those included within 180 days stayed at 5 to 7. Included methods more often changed one part of the existing loss and more often came with experiments on large policies, while released code was as common among them as among the others. Merged pull requests drew concerns about design and tests as well, while concerns about demand and maintenance burden appeared mostly in proposals that were not merged. Yet few methods were turned away in public, because most never reached frameworks issues or pull requests at all. Users rarely report training failures in those issues, and the technical reports of large open-weight models state the methods that most frameworks include, so the public record of demand is thin and the record of practice at scale overlaps with the frameworks code. Other fields with shared training or evaluation code can reuse this measurement, since it needs only paper versions, implementation histories and public proposals. The tracker lists where each framework keeps its algorithms, the concerns its reviewers raised and the outcome of earlier proposals, so that authors can bring method that far.

sections.content: Each paper receives exactly one label from its title and abstract. An RL method is general when the component is the papers main contribution and is presented for RL with language models at large. sections.title: E The public record
sections.content: The record covers 26,960 issues, pull requests and discussions downloaded through the GitHub API on 18 October 2026 (UTC), after the framework snapshots in Table 10. Every discussion was read in full, and none had more comments than one request returns. Formal review texts were read for the coded threads and the landing pull requests only. thread matches paper through link to its arXiv, Hugging Face papers or alphaXiv page, its identifier after arXiv:, its bare identifier, or its full title of at least five words. Identifiers are checked against the pool, so every match names pool paper. The separate search by method name uses names of at least four characters with capital letter that occur once in the pool, and every match for paper without record was read in its thread. The citation audit reads every line added on each main branch and keeps the first commit that cites paper in each file. All files citing paper were checked by hand. Of the 23 general methods cited in 21 framework files but missed by parsing, 9 sit next to an implementation, including the NeMo-RL fix to the KL gradient and ROLLs trajectory-level agent pipeline. Another 10 appear in lists of projects or news, 2 in reference lists of technical report PDFs read as text, and 2 as configuration note or background reference. Each proposal thread received one outcome and the reasons maintainer stated explicitly in it, coded from the threads own text. first reader coded all threads, and second reader coded them again blind to the first coding. The analysis uses the blind codes. The two codings agree on the outcome of 40 of 48 threads as raw agreement, and most differences concern redirects and withdrawals. Outcomes follow fixed order. proposer who closes the thread has withdrawn it. maintainer who sends the proposal to an example, an experimental folder or separate repository has redirected it. An explicit refusal is decline, and closure by scheduled rule is stale cleanup. When several threads in one framework concern the same paper, such as withdrawn first attempt and its replacement, we code the main thread. Demand covers the number of requests, reactions and implementations elsewhere. Maintenance burden covers new options, trainers or interfaces to keep. Placement covers move to an experimental folder, recipe, an example or separate repository. Evidence covers results to reproduce or gains to show. The other reasons are missing tests or documentation, an objection to the interface or architecture of the change, and an existing feature that already covers the case. stated reason is also concern in the review fields of the same thread, and one adjudication resolved the two threads where the codings first disagreed. The review fields of Table 3 were coded for every merged landing pull request and every proposal with one set of rules. concern counts when someone other than the proposer raises it explicitly, and requests about style or naming do not count. An open concern is one the thread leaves unaddressed at its end, including follow-up work named at the merge. The failure reading of Section 8 screened every issue and discussion opened since 1 January 2025 with keyword patterns for the thirteen failures of the catalog. The patterns were applied to the title and the first 800 characters of the opening post after removing code blocks, logs and configuration lines. One reader coded each of the 648 matches as failure report with the failure named, bug, usage question, feature request or other. method request is thread that asks for named method. The recall sample draws 250 unscreened threads at random with fixed seed, and the release keeps each coded threads number, title, keywords and code. The report reading of Section 9 takes every model report in the pool for an open-weight model with 100B or more total parameters, reads its RL sections in the latest arXiv version, and keeps one quote per report with the methods it states. Reports that mention RL only in the body are outside the pool. Among the open-weight models with 100B or more parameters released in the window, the reports of Qwen3 [81], Pangu Ultra MoE [68], Intern-S1 [3], Command [71], dots.llm1 [30] and Step-3 [67] fall outside it.
